title: Back to the table
text: A few weeks ago my fourteen-year-old nephew announced, with the air of someone revealing a state secret, that he wanted a board game for his birthday. I nearly dropped my cup. This is a boy who can talk for an hour about the latest video game, yet there he stood, asking for a box of cardboard and plastic tokens. My first thought was that someone had put him up to it. My second, rather more humbling thought was that I had been behind the times for several years. I am hardly a stranger to games myself, but for years I had regarded a pack of cards as something to be kept in a drawer for emergencies.

It turns out that he is far from alone. Sales of board games have been rising steadily, and cafés where customers can borrow a game and play for hours are opening in many cities. The reasons are not hard to find. After days of staring at screens, people crave something they can touch: dice, cards, small wooden pieces. There is also the pleasure of sitting across a table from a real face, with all its raised eyebrows and unconvincing poker expressions, instead of an avatar. A shop owner I spoke to told me that her best customers are not children but people in their thirties, who arrive straight from work and stay until closing time.

What surprised me most was how clever the new games are. The old classics, which depend on luck and last until somebody storms off, have been joined by designs in which players cooperate against the board itself. In one popular game, everybody must work together to stop a disease from spreading, and nobody can **call the shots** alone. I was sceptical, but after an evening of arguing about strategy with my nephew and his friends, I found myself genuinely anxious about a make-believe epidemic.

Of course, there is a practical side as well. A video game demands a device, a connection and, quite often, a subscription, whereas a board game needs only a table and a few willing friends. It can be played on a rainy afternoon, on a long train journey or during a power cut, and the same box can entertain a family for years. In an age of constant updates, that kind of reliability feels almost luxurious. My neighbours, who own a battered copy of a game from the 1980s, claim that they have never finished an evening without a dispute, and that this is precisely the point.

Not everyone is persuaded. Critics point out that learning the rules can take an hour, during which half the guests quietly lose interest, and that some games are expensive enough to make a strategic mistake feel like a financial one. There is some truth in both complaints. Yet the same people tend to admit that they enjoyed themselves once the pieces were on the table, which suggests that the real obstacle is a mild reluctance to begin rather than the games themselves.

I do not believe that board games will replace screens, nor should they. But I have come to see their return as a quiet protest against doing everything alone, in silence, at arm's length from other people. Two hours around a table, laughing at a bad decision or groaning at a bad throw of the dice, turned out to be better entertainment than I expected, and my nephew, who won, was kind enough not to mention it more than twice. Next month, as it happens, I have been invited to a family tournament, and I have already begun to practise in secret.

questions.q: Why was the author surprised by her nephew's request?
options: He rarely asks for presents.
He disliked the games she suggested.
He normally prefers computer games.
He had nobody to play with.

questions.q: What do 'both complaints' in paragraph 5 refer to?
options: Learning the rules is slow and some games are dear.
Games are noisy and tiring.
Rules are unfair and prices keep rising.
Games are childish and boring.
make a lucky guess.
take all the decisions.
start an argument.
lose control.

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, why do people turn to board games?
options: They cost less than going out.
They give people a rest from work.
They are easier to learn than video games.
They offer physical objects and personal contact.

questions.q: How did the author react to the cooperative game?
options: She was doubtful at first but became involved.
She refused to take part.
She thought it was too easy.
She preferred the old classics.

questions.q: Which advantage of board games is NOT mentioned in the text?
options: They can be played without electricity.
They bring people together.
They improve players' memory.
They can be enjoyed for many years.

questions.q: The author concludes that board games …
options: are better than any screen entertainment.
offer a pleasant way of spending time together.
should be taught at school.
will soon go out of fashion again.
